name: Cash Conversion Cycle
description: Adds days inventory outstanding and days sales outstanding, then subtracts days payables outstanding, to show how many days cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.
notes: A shorter or negative cycle means cash is freed up faster or suppliers effectively finance operations. All three inputs must be measured over the same period and in days.

name: Sell-through Rate
description: Expresses the percentage of received inventory that was sold within a period, as units sold divided by units received times 100. Selling 180 of 300 received units gives a 60% sell-through rate.
notes: Both counts should cover the same period and product. A rate near 100% may signal understocking, while a low rate suggests overstock or weak demand.

name: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
description: Divides total marketing and sales spending by the number of new customers acquired to find the average cost of gaining one customer. Spending 50000 to gain 250 customers yields a CAC of 200 per customer.
notes: Include all marketing and sales costs for the period, and count only genuinely new customers. Compare against customer lifetime value to judge whether acquisition is profitable.

name: Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
description: Estimates the total revenue one customer generates over their relationship, as average order value times purchases per year times average lifespan in years. Here 120×4×3 gives an LTV of 1440.
notes: This simple form uses revenue and ignores gross margin, discounting and retention decay, so it tends to overstate true profit-based lifetime value.

name: LTV to CAC Ratio
description: Divides customer lifetime value by customer acquisition cost to show how much value each acquired customer returns per unit of acquisition spend. An LTV of 1440 against a CAC of 200 gives a ratio of 7.2.
notes: A common health benchmark is around 3 or higher; a very high ratio may indicate underinvestment in growth. Use consistent LTV and CAC definitions (both revenue or both margin based).

name: Churn Rate
description: Gives the percentage of customers lost during a period, as customers lost divided by customers at the start times 100. Losing 50 of 1000 starting customers is a 5% churn rate.
notes: The denominator is the count at the start of the period, and new customers gained during the period are excluded. Retention rate is 100 minus this value.

name: Conversion Rate
description: Expresses the share of visitors who completed a desired action, as conversions divided by visitors times 100. With 320 conversions from 8000 visitors the conversion rate is 4%.
notes: Define a conversion consistently (purchase, signup, etc.) and count unique visitors over the same window to avoid inflating or deflating the rate.

name: Average Order Value (AOV)
description: Divides total revenue by the number of orders to find the average amount spent per order. Revenue of 96000 across 800 orders gives an AOV of 120.
notes: Use the same period for both figures and decide consistently whether revenue includes tax, shipping and refunds, since that changes the result.

name: Return on Ad Spend (ROAS)
description: Divides revenue attributed to advertising by the amount spent on those ads to show revenue earned per unit of ad spend. Revenue of 120000 on 30000 of spend gives a ROAS of 4.
notes: ROAS is a revenue ratio, not profit; it ignores product cost and margins, so a ROAS above 1 does not guarantee overall profitability.

name: Cost per Mille (CPM)
description: Gives the advertising cost per one thousand impressions, as ad cost divided by impressions times 1000. A cost of 4500 over 900000 impressions is a CPM of 5.
notes: Mille means one thousand, hence the ×1000 scaling. CPM measures cost of reach only and says nothing about clicks or conversions.

name: Cost per Click (CPC)
description: Divides advertising cost by the number of clicks to find the average price paid for each click. Spending 4500 for 3000 clicks gives a CPC of 1.50.
notes: CPC covers clicks only, not conversions or sales, so a low CPC is not automatically efficient if those clicks do not convert.

name: Rule of 40 (SaaS)

variables.label: Profit margin, e.g. FCF or EBITDA (%)

description: Adds revenue growth and profit margin; software companies above 40 % are considered healthy.
notes: Lets fast-growing loss-makers and slower profitable firms be compared on one scale.

name: Burn Multiple
description: Divides net cash burned by net new annual recurring revenue added in the same period (Sacks 2020).
notes: Below 1 is excellent, above 2 suspect.

name: Cash Runway
description: Gives how many months a company can operate before its cash runs out at the current burn rate.
notes: Start-ups usually raise money when about 12–18 months remain.

name: Net Revenue Retention
description: Gives the share of recurring revenue kept from existing customers after a year, including upsells.
notes: Above 100 % means the customer base grows even without new customers.

name: CAC Payback Period
description: Gives the months of gross profit needed to earn back the cost of acquiring a customer.
notes: SaaS companies aim for under 12–18 months.

name: Customer Lifetime Value (Churn-Based)
description: Estimates lifetime gross profit per customer as margin per month divided by the monthly churn rate.
notes: Average customer lifetime is 1/churn months (50 months here).

name: SaaS Quick Ratio
description: Computes the SaaS quick ratio: recurring revenue added divided by recurring revenue lost in the same period.
notes: MRR is monthly recurring revenue. A value above 4 is often cited as efficient growth.

name: SaaS Magic Number

variables.label: Sales and marketing spend last quarter

description: Computes the magic number, the annualised growth in quarterly revenue per unit of last quarter's sales and marketing spend.
notes: Values above about 0.75 are commonly read as a sign that more sales spending is worthwhile.

name: Gross Revenue Retention
description: Computes gross revenue retention, the share of starting recurring revenue kept after downgrades and cancellations, without counting expansion.
notes: It can never exceed 100 %; net revenue retention adds expansion revenue.

name: Customer Retention Rate
description: Computes the share of customers at the start of a period who are still customers at its end.
notes: New customers are subtracted so that growth does not hide losses.

name: Sales Velocity
description: Computes sales velocity, the revenue a sales pipeline produces per day.
notes: Raising the number of opportunities, the win rate or the deal size, or shortening the cycle, raises velocity.

name: Sales Volume Increase Needed after a Price Cut
description: Computes how much more must be sold after a price cut to keep the same total gross profit.
notes: The cut must be smaller than the margin. With a 40 % margin a 10 % cut needs one third more volume.

name: Sales Volume Loss Allowed after a Price Rise
description: Computes how much sales volume can fall after a price rise before total gross profit drops.
notes: If volume falls by less than this, the price rise increases gross profit.

name: Viral Coefficient (K-Factor)
description: Computes the viral coefficient, the number of new users each user brings in.
notes: A value above 1 means each generation of users is larger than the last.

name: Average Customer Lifetime from Churn
description: Computes the average customer lifetime as the reciprocal of the churn rate, assuming churn stays constant.
notes: With a monthly churn rate the result is in months.

name: Email List Growth Rate
description: Computes the net growth of a mailing list over a period as a percentage of its starting size.
notes: Count unsubscribes, spam complaints and hard bounces as losses.

name: Leads Needed for a Revenue Target
description: Computes how many leads a sales funnel needs to reach a revenue target, working back from the deal size and the conversion rates.
notes: Rates come from the funnel's own history; round the result up.

name: Revenue per Visitor
description: Computes the average revenue each website visitor brings, combining the conversion rate and the average order value.
notes: Useful for comparing the value of traffic sources or the effect of a test on both conversion and order size.
